author: Baranidaran Palanivelu
headline: Senior Data Analyst @ ICON plc
text:
I asked a SQL question in a Data Analyst interview .

Not "write a query." Not "what's the syntax."

Just this:
"You're joining orders to customers to calculate monthly revenue. Which JOIN do you use — and why?"

Some candidates said INNER JOIN immediately.

One candidate paused.
Then said:

"Depends. If I use INNER JOIN, I silently drop every customer who placed no orders. My revenue base looks cleaner — but it's wrong. I'd use LEFT JOIN and then flag the nulls separately."

The other candidates never thought about what they were losing.

She wasn't just writing SQL. She was protecting a business decision from bad data.

That's the difference between someone who knows SQL and someone who understands it.

Here's the scenario:

You're calculating monthly active users. Users table LEFT JOIN or INNER JOIN to activity table?

Which do you use — and what do you lose if you get it wrong?

👇 Be specific. I'll reply to every answer.
♻️ Repost — someone preparing for SQL interviews needs this today.

author: Surbhi Goyal
headline: 100k+ LinkedIn Family | NIT Graduate | 1000+ Resume | Mentor | Spark | Scala | PySpark | Hadoop | Hive | HBase | Azure | AWS | Matillion
text:
I’ve been in the data domain for 9+ years, and 1 thing has remained constant throughout… 

SQL.

Over the years, these are the most commonly asked SQL topics and questions I’ve come across 👇

1️⃣ JOINS
→ INNER vs LEFT vs RIGHT vs FULL (with use cases)
→ Join vs Subquery — when to use what
→ Finding unmatched records between tables
→ Real-world use cases of self joins

2️⃣ GROUP BY & AGGREGATIONS
→ GROUP BY vs HAVING
→ Second / nth highest salary problems
→ COUNT vs COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column)
→ Conditional aggregations

3️⃣ WINDOW FUNCTIONS
→ ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK
→ Finding the latest record per group
→ Running totals & cumulative metrics
→ PARTITION BY vs GROUP BY

4️⃣ SUBQUERIES & CTEs
→ CTE vs Subquery (performance + readability)
→ Nested subqueries
→ Basics of recursive CTEs

5️⃣ DATE & TIME
→ Date vs Timestamp
→ Queries for last N days
→ Month-over-month comparisons
→ Handling time zones

6️⃣ DATA CLEANING
→ Handling NULL values
→ Deduplication strategies
→ Identifying duplicates
→ Using CASE statements

Every interviewer has a different style, but these patterns repeat again and again.

That said, SQL is just one part of the puzzle.

To crack Data Engineering roles, you also need a strong grasp of ETL pipelines, Big Data, and cloud platforms. And this is where many people get stuck… either in a prep loop or without a clear direction.

That’s why learning with the right structure and guidance can make a huge difference.

author: PRAVEEN SINGH
headline: 🚀 44k+ LinkedIns ✅ Open For Collabs🤝|☁️ AWS Data Engineer 🚀| AI | AWS(5+ yr) | | Python · PySpark · Pandas . AWS (S3, Redshift, Glue, Athena)
text:
🚨 Stop Writing Slow SQL — Use Python Like a Data Engineer 🚀

If you’re still relying ONLY on SQL for heavy data transformations… you’re already behind.

Top Data Engineers don’t just write queries.
They combine SQL + Python to build scalable, production-ready pipelines.

Here’s one HIGHLY recommended topic you must master 👇

🔥 “SQL + Python Integration for Data Processing”

Why this matters:
👉 SQL is great for querying
👉 Python is powerful for transformation, automation & scaling
👉 Together = 🔥 unstoppable data pipelines

💡 Example: Read SQL data → Process in Python → Optimize → Store back

import pandas as pd
import sqlalchemy

Step 1: Connect to database
engine = sqlalchemy.create_engine("postgresql://user:password@localhost:5432/db")

Step 2: Read data using SQL
query = """
SELECT department, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 50000;
"""
df = pd.read_sql(query, engine)

Step 3: Python transformation (more flexible than SQL)
df['bonus'] = df['salary'] * 0.10

Step 4: Write back to database
df.to_sql("employee_bonus", engine, if_exists="replace", index=False)

print("Data pipeline executed successfully 🚀")

⚡ Why Data Engineers love this approach:
✔ Handles complex transformations easily
✔ Works with big data tools (PySpark, Airflow)
✔ Automates pipelines end-to-end
✔ Improves performance beyond raw SQL

🎯 Pro Tip:
Master this stack:
👉 SQL (for querying)
👉 Python (for logic & automation)
👉 PySpark (for big data scale)

If you want to become a top 1% Data Engineer, stop choosing between SQL and Python…

text:
Interviewers know within first 15 minutes whether a Senior Data Engineer truly understands SQL or PySpark.

𝗣𝗮𝗿𝘁 4 – KING OF ALL SCD2

Stop manually handling Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD Type 2) with messy, multi-step scripts. 🛑
If you’re working with Delta Lake, you can handle historical versioning in a single, atomic MERGE operation.

Here is a breakdown of how this Python function implements a Type 2 Upsert during a streaming micro-batch:
🔹 The "Secret Sauce" (The Union):

 To handle an SCD Type 2, you need to do two things at once:
🔹Expire the old record (Update).
🔹Insert the new record (Insert).

 By unioning the updates with a "null-key" version of themselves, we force the MERGE engine to treat the new data as both a match (to close the old record) and a non-match (to create the new one).

🔹 The Logic:
MATCHED: If the price has changed, we set current = false and add an end_date.
NOT MATCHED: We insert the new record as the new "truth" with current = true.

This pattern ensures your silver table maintains a perfect history of every price change without duplicating rows or losing track of the past.

text:
🚀 Data Engineer Interview at Deloitte (3+ Years Exp) — What They Actually Check
Most candidates prepare tools.

Smart candidates prepare thinking.
Recently, one of my 3+ years experienced students cracked a Data Engineer round at Deloitte — and here’s what really made the difference 👇

❌ Not fancy buzzwords
❌ Not 50 tools on a resume

✅ Strong fundamentals + real-world scenarios
💡 These were the game-changer areas:
✔️ Designing data pipelines for 10M+ records/day

→ They weren’t testing tools… they were testing your architecture mindset
✔️ ETL vs ELT — when and why?
→ Not textbook definitions — real project justification matters

✔️ Spark performance tuning
→ Partitioning, caching, broadcast joins — explain with use cases
✔️ SQL deep dive (beyond basics)
→ Window functions, query optimization, rewrites — show depth

✔️ Failure handling in pipelines
→ Retry logic, checkpointing, idempotency — think production-ready systems
✔️ Cloud stack (ADF / Databricks / S3 / Glue)

→ Focus on how you used them, not just what they are
🎯 What impressed the interviewer most?
Instead of saying:
“I used Spark + ADF + SQL”

He explained:

👉 Why Spark was chosen
👉 What problem it solved
👉 What alternatives were considered
👉 Trade-offs and impact
🔥 That’s the difference between knowing 
tools and thinking like an engineer.
If you're preparing for Data Engineer roles:
👉 Stop memorizing. Start explaining your decisions.
